reader.title: Killing of Gus Saddler
bases: A crowd of citizens seized a Black man accused of raping a white child, put a rope round his neck to force a confession, and he was shot dead by an unknown person while still in their hands (A1, A2, A3).

He was killed without lawful authority after a crowd of citizens seized him, staged a mock hanging and extracted a confession to an alleged rape (A1, A2, A3); the papers attribute the fatal shot to a single 'unknown party' within or near that crowd, so the group's part in the killing itself is inferred rather than stated (A2, A3).

Two Lake Charles papers, each citing its own reporter, agree on the arrest by citizens, the confession, the fatal shot by an unknown person and the coroner's verdict (A1, A2), and the St. Landry Democrat and a Police Jury inquest payment confirm it (A3, A4).

summary.text: The killing of Gus Saddler was the shooting of a young Black man by an unknown person at Bagdad, Calcasieu Parish, Louisiana, on September 2, 1888, while he was held by a crowd of local citizens.
The crowd had seized him after he was accused of raping a six-year-old white girl and forced a confession from him by staging a mock hanging.
A coroner's jury found that he had been killed by an unknown party, and the Lake Charles Commercial presented the death as "Swift Retribution."
According to the Lake Charles Commercial, Saddler was about 19 years old and had come to the area a few months earlier from St. Landry Parish.
The Lake Charles Echo called him Gus Williams and said he had come "from about Washington, La."
The Commercial and the St. Landry Democrat reported that he was accused of sexually assaulting a six-year-old white girl on Saturday, September 1, and of threatening to kill her if she told anyone.
The girl told her parents the next day, and word of the accusation spread on Sunday evening.
Within a few hours, according to the Commercial, many citizens of West Lake Charles and Bagdad gathered and seized him.
In the Commercial's account, they "tied him hard" and put a rope around his neck, pretending they were going to hang him in order to make him confess, "which he did fully."
The Echo said only that he was arrested and "confessed his guilt," without mentioning the rope.
As the crowd set out to take him to jail, or, as the Commercial and the Democrat put it, to turn him over to the sheriff, someone fired at him.
The shot struck him in the head and killed him instantly; his body was later found near Grout's shingle mill in Bagdad.
Coroner A. J. Perkins viewed the body on Monday morning, and on Tuesday a coroner's jury heard sixteen witnesses.

The Commercial gave the verdict as "death caused by a shot through the head by an unknown party," while the Echo described it as death from a pistol or gunshot wound "in the hands of unknown parties."
His body was turned over to relatives, who sent it to St. Landry Parish.

In December, the Calcasieu Police Jury paid Perkins $30 for holding the inquest and post-mortem examination on "Gus. Saddler, Sept. 4, 1888," and paid five men $2 each for a day's service on the jury.
The coverage reports no arrest of the shooter or of anyone in the crowd.
Only local and home-parish white papers carried the story.
The Lake Charles Echo ran a plain paragraph on September 7, giving the case through "an Echo reporter" and naming the dead man as Gus Williams.

The next day the Lake Charles Commercial ran a longer item headed "A Brutal Crime and Swift Retribution." It called the alleged assault "one of the most heinous crimes known" and blamed "a burly negro," and it described the mock hanging without criticism.
On September 15 the St. Landry Democrat, in Saddler's former home parish, ran a short version that described him as "colored, formerly of this parish."
All three papers stated the rape accusation as fact and rested it on the confession the crowd had obtained.
The Saddler inquest surfaced again only as a line in the Police Jury's expense list, printed in both Lake Charles papers in December.
The papers disagreed on the dead man's surname: the Echo printed "Gus Williams," while the Commercial, the St. Landry Democrat and the Police Jury's payment record all gave "Saddler."
They also differed over whether the confession was coerced, since only the Commercial and the Democrat reported the rope and the pretended hanging.

accounts.label: Lake Charles Echo reporter
accounts.gist: Citizens met to find who had raped a little white girl, arrested Gus Williams, who 'confessed his guilt', and as the crowd started to jail with him he was fired upon by someone unknown.

accounts.label: Lake Charles Commercial reporter
accounts.gist: Citizens tied Gus Saddler and put a rope round his neck, pretending to hang him to make him confess; as they were about to turn him over to the sheriff an unknown party shot him through the head.

accounts.label: St. Landry Democrat
accounts.gist: Repeats the rope-and-confession account and the shot by an unknown person as he was being turned over to the sheriff, identifying him as formerly of St. Landry parish.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Death by a pistol or gunshot wound, or a shot through the head, at the hands of unknown parties or an unknown party.

framing.detail: The Echo gave the killing in a flat local paragraph, treating the alleged rape and confession as established and the shooter as 'some one unknown'.
The Commercial headlined 'A Brutal Crime and Swift Retribution', called the crime 'one of the most heinous crimes known' by 'a burly negro', and described the mock hanging without criticism.
The St. Landry Democrat stated as fact that Saddler 'committed rape' and reported the shooting in a short paragraph without comment.

conflicts.note: Two newspapers and the Police Jury's inquest payment record use Saddler; the official payment entry is the stronger evidence.
